questions.stem: An office is best described as a place where
options: information is received, recorded, processed, stored and given out
questions.explanation: The office is the information centre of an organisation.

questions.stem: The number of subordinates a manager can supervise effectively is known as the

questions.stem: Which is a DISADVANTAGE of the open-plan office?
options: Noise and lack of privacy for confidential work
questions.explanation: Open-plan offices can be noisy and offer little privacy.

questions.stem: A standard way of carrying out a recurring office task, such as dealing with incoming invoices, is called an office
questions.explanation: Office procedures set out the steps for routine tasks so they are done consistently.

questions.stem: Which of these is a function of the office?
questions.explanation: Record keeping is a core office function.

questions.explanation: Public relations manages the image of the organisation.

questions.stem: Which department is responsible for converting raw materials into finished goods?
questions.explanation: The production department manufactures the goods.

questions.stem: A machine used to punch holes in papers so that they can be placed in a file is a

questions.stem: Which of the following is an electrical office machine?
questions.explanation: A photocopier runs on electricity; the others are manual.

questions.stem: A machine that sends an exact copy of a document through a telephone line is a
questions.explanation: Fax machines transmit document images over telephone lines.

questions.stem: Which of these is good care of office equipment?
options: Allowing untrained staff to repair machines
Placing machines near open windows in the rain
Covering machines after use and servicing them regularly
questions.explanation: Covering and regular servicing prolong the life of equipment.

questions.explanation: Duplicators and photocopiers produce many copies quickly.

questions.stem: A main advantage of using a computer instead of a manual typewriter is that
options: documents can be edited and saved before printing
it cannot be damaged by viruses
questions.explanation: Computers allow easy correction, storage and reuse of documents.

questions.stem: The first point of contact for visitors to an organisation is the

questions.stem: The book in which a receptionist records the names and times of arrival of visitors is the
questions.explanation: The visitors' register keeps a record of callers.

questions.stem: Which quality is MOST important for a receptionist?
questions.explanation: The receptionist creates the first impression of the organisation.

questions.stem: A card given to a regular visitor or business partner, which shows the person's name and business details, is a
questions.explanation: Business cards help the receptionist to record and announce callers correctly.

questions.stem: When answering an office telephone, the receptionist should first
options: ask the caller to call back later
transfer the call immediately without speaking
greet the caller and state the name of the organisation
questions.explanation: A polite greeting with the organisation's name is standard telephone procedure.

options: take a message accurately and pass it on promptly
tell the caller the manager does not want to speak

questions.stem: An application form for employment and a staff leave form are examples of
questions.explanation: They relate to the administration of staff, not to buying, selling or stores.

questions.stem: A short written message sent from one department to another within the same organisation is a
questions.explanation: A memo is used for internal communication.

questions.stem: A letter of the same content sent to many people at the same time is a
questions.explanation: Circulars carry the same information to many recipients.

questions.stem: In a business letter, the part that gives the recipient's name and address is the
questions.explanation: The inside address is placed on the left above the salutation.

questions.stem: A business letter beginning "Dear Sir" usually ends with
questions.explanation: "Dear Sir/Madam" is matched with "Yours faithfully"; a named salutation uses "Yours sincerely".

questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT normally appear on a memorandum?
questions.explanation: Memos omit the salutation and complimentary close used in letters.

questions.stem: The written record of what was discussed and decided at a meeting is the
questions.explanation: Minutes record proceedings and decisions.

questions.stem: The printed name, address and logo of a firm at the top of its letter paper is the
questions.explanation: The letterhead identifies the sender's organisation.

questions.stem: Letters received by an organisation are called
questions.explanation: Mail arriving from outside is incoming mail.

questions.stem: An envelope marked "Confidential" addressed to the manager should be
options: opened by the mail clerk and read
questions.explanation: Confidential and personal mail is delivered unopened.

questions.stem: The first step in handling incoming mail is to
questions.explanation: Mail is sorted (e.g. personal, confidential, urgent, ordinary) before opening.

questions.stem: Stamping incoming letters with the date of receipt helps the organisation to
questions.explanation: The date stamp provides evidence of when mail was received.

questions.stem: A machine that prints postage impressions on envelopes instead of using adhesive stamps is a
questions.explanation: Franking machines print the postage paid on outgoing mail.

questions.stem: A book in which outgoing letters and the postage spent on them are recorded is the
questions.explanation: The postage book controls stamp usage.

questions.stem: When an incoming letter mentions an enclosure that is missing, the mail clerk should
options: note the omission on the letter and inform the sender or the officer concerned

questions.stem: Filing is the
options: systematic arrangement and storage of documents so they can be found easily
questions.explanation: Filing keeps records orderly and accessible.

questions.stem: Arranging files according to the first letter of the names of correspondents is
questions.explanation: Alphabetical filing uses the A-Z order of names.

questions.stem: Arranging documents according to date is
questions.explanation: Chronological filing orders papers by date.

questions.stem: A company with branches in many states files correspondence by state and town. This is
questions.explanation: Geographical filing is arranged by location.

questions.stem: Numerical filing requires a separate index because
options: it cannot be used for large files
the files are known by numbers, not by names
it is only used for confidential files
questions.explanation: An alphabetical index links names to file numbers.

questions.stem: In lateral filing, files are
options: placed one behind another in drawers
stored side by side on shelves, like books
questions.explanation: Lateral filing stores files sideways on shelves or racks.

questions.stem: Which filing system saves the most office space and allows quick searching of documents?
questions.explanation: Electronic files take little physical space and can be searched by computer.

questions.stem: When a file is removed from the filing cabinet, an "out card" (absent card) is placed in its position to
options: show who has borrowed the file and when
questions.explanation: Out cards help to trace files that have been taken out.

questions.stem: Communication is the
options: transfer of information from a sender to a receiver
questions.explanation: Communication is the passing of a message so that it is understood.

questions.stem: A face-to-face discussion between a manager and a worker is an example of
questions.explanation: Spoken communication is oral.

questions.stem: Nodding the head, gestures and facial expressions are examples of
questions.explanation: Body language communicates without words.

questions.stem: The public organisation that provides postal services in Nigeria is
questions.explanation: NIPOST is the Nigerian Postal Service.

questions.stem: Charts, graphs and posters are forms of
questions.explanation: They communicate by sight.

questions.stem: Television is classified as which type of communication medium?
questions.explanation: TV carries both sound and pictures.

questions.stem: A manager in Lagos holds a meeting with branch managers in Kano and Port Harcourt, all seeing one another on screens. This is
questions.explanation: Video conferencing uses cameras and screens with sound.

questions.stem: A list of items to be discussed at a meeting is the
questions.explanation: The agenda sets out the order of business.

questions.stem: The minimum number of members that must be present for a meeting to be valid is the
questions.explanation: Without a quorum, decisions are not valid.

questions.stem: A meeting of shareholders held once every year to receive the accounts and elect directors is the
questions.explanation: The AGM is held yearly as required by company law.

questions.stem: In the order of business of a meeting, "matters arising" comes
options: after the reading and adoption of the last minutes
questions.explanation: Matters arising come from the minutes just adopted.

questions.stem: AOB on an agenda stands for
questions.explanation: AOB allows items not listed to be raised at the end.

questions.stem: A meeting called at short notice to deal with an urgent problem is a(n)
questions.explanation: Emergency (extraordinary) meetings deal with urgent matters.

questions.stem: The duty of keeping order and ensuring that the meeting follows the agenda belongs to the
questions.explanation: The chairman controls the meeting; the secretary records it.

questions.stem: Postponing a meeting to a later date is called
questions.explanation: An adjourned meeting is continued at a later time.

questions.stem: A report is a
options: list of items for a meeting
formal written account of facts and findings on a subject
questions.explanation: Reports present information and findings, often with recommendations.

questions.stem: A report produced at regular intervals, such as a monthly sales report, is a
questions.explanation: Routine reports are made regularly.

questions.stem: The part of a report that gives the writer's suggestions for action is the
questions.explanation: Recommendations state what should be done.

questions.stem: A report prepared after looking into the causes of a fire in a company's warehouse is a(n)
questions.explanation: It investigates a particular incident.

questions.stem: The section of a report that states the scope and purpose given to the writer is the
questions.explanation: Terms of reference define what the report must cover.

questions.stem: Information that reaches the user in time for a decision to be made is described as
questions.explanation: Timeliness is a quality of good information.

questions.stem: Which of these is a primary source of information?
questions.explanation: Primary information is collected first-hand.

questions.stem: Which quality of good information means that it is free from errors?
questions.explanation: Accurate information is correct.

questions.stem: Storing information on flash drives, hard disks and cloud servers is an example of
questions.explanation: These store information in digital form.

questions.stem: A manager receives a detailed 80-page report when she only needs the total monthly sales figure. The report lacks the quality of
questions.explanation: Good information should be relevant and usable for the decision required.

questions.stem:
(a) Define an office. [2 marks]
(b) State five functions of the office. [10 marks]
(c) Explain the following principles of office organisation: (i) span of control; (ii) unity of command; (iii) unity of function; (iv) delegation of authority. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) a place where information is received, recorded, processed, stored and given out for the administration of an organisation
10 marks: (b) any five, 2 marks each: receiving information; recording information; processing/arranging information; storing information; giving out information; safeguarding assets; communication; coordination
2 marks: (c)(i) span of control: the number of subordinates a superior can effectively supervise
2 marks: (c)(ii) unity of command: each subordinate receives orders from only one superior
2 marks: (c)(iii) unity of function: related activities are grouped together under one head
2 marks: (c)(iv) delegation: passing authority to a subordinate to perform a task while responsibility remains with the superior
questions.explanation: An office is the information centre of an organisation. Functions: receiving, recording, processing, storing and giving information, and safeguarding assets. Span of control limits subordinates per manager; unity of command means one boss; unity of function groups similar tasks; delegation passes authority down.

questions.stem:
(a) List five departments found in a large manufacturing organisation. [5 marks]
(b) State three functions of each of the following departments: (i) personnel; (ii) accounts; (iii) sales. [9 marks]
(c) State three uses of an organisational chart. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a) any five: production, personnel/HR, accounts, sales/marketing, purchasing, administration, transport, public relations, legal, research (1 mark each)
3 marks: (b)(i) personnel: recruitment and selection; training; staff welfare; discipline; records (any three, 1 mark each)
3 marks: (b)(ii) accounts: keeping financial records; payroll; paying suppliers; preparing final accounts; budgets (any three, 1 mark each)
3 marks: (b)(iii) sales: selling goods; advertising; market research; handling orders; after-sales service (any three, 1 mark each)
6 marks: (c) any three, 2 marks each: shows lines of authority; shows departments and their relationships; helps new staff understand the structure; shows span of control; helps identify duplication
questions.explanation: Departments include production, personnel, accounts, sales, purchasing and administration. Personnel recruits, trains and cares for staff; accounts keeps records and pays salaries; sales sells and advertises. The organisational chart shows authority lines, structure and relationships.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain the meaning of office equipment. [2 marks]
(b) State the use of each of the following: (i) photocopier; (ii) shredding machine; (iii) franking machine; (iv) scanner; (v) perforator. [10 marks]
(c) State four ways of taking care of office equipment. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) machines and tools used in the office to make work easier, faster and more accurate
2 marks: (b)(i) photocopier: makes exact copies of documents
2 marks: (b)(ii) shredder: destroys confidential documents by cutting them into strips
2 marks: (b)(iii) franking machine: prints postage impressions on outgoing mail
2 marks: (b)(iv) scanner: converts paper documents and images into digital form
2 marks: (b)(v) perforator: punches holes in papers for filing
8 marks: (c) any four, 2 marks each: cover after use; regular servicing; use by trained staff; follow manufacturer's instructions; keep in a clean, dry place; switch off after use; use stabilisers
questions.explanation: Office equipment are tools and machines that make office work easier. Photocopiers copy, shredders destroy, franking machines print postage, scanners digitise and perforators punch holes. Care includes covering, servicing, trained users, following instructions, and switching off after use.

questions.stem:
(a) State five duties of a receptionist. [10 marks]
(b) State five qualities of a good receptionist. [5 marks]
(c) Outline the procedure a receptionist should follow when receiving a telephone call for an officer who is absent. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: (a) any five, 2 marks each: receiving and welcoming visitors; keeping the visitors' register; handling telephone calls; keeping the appointments diary; directing visitors; giving information about the organisation; handling enquiries; receiving parcels
5 marks: (b) any five: polite; neat appearance; good memory; patient; good communication skills; tactful; honest; knowledgeable about the organisation (1 mark each)
5 marks: (c) greet and identify the organisation; inform the caller that the officer is absent; take the caller's name, number and message; read the message back to confirm; pass the message promptly to the officer (1 mark each)
questions.explanation: The receptionist welcomes and directs visitors, keeps registers and diaries, handles calls and enquiries. Qualities: courtesy, neatness, patience, tact, communication skill. For an absent officer: greet, explain, take a full message, confirm it and deliver it promptly.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between incoming and outgoing mail. [4 marks]
(b) Describe the procedure for handling incoming mail in a large organisation. [10 marks]
(c) State three ways of sending outgoing mail. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) incoming mail is received by the organisation from outside
2 marks: (a) outgoing mail is sent out by the organisation
10 marks: (b) any five steps, 2 marks each: collect and sort the mail; deliver personal/confidential mail unopened; open other mail with a letter opener; check enclosures; date-stamp each letter; record in the incoming mail register; distribute to departments; attach previous correspondence
6 marks: (c) any three, 2 marks each: ordinary post; registered post; courier service; e-mail; express/speed post; hand delivery by dispatch rider
questions.explanation: Incoming mail comes in; outgoing goes out. Handling: collect and sort, pass confidential items unopened, open, check enclosures, date-stamp, register and distribute. Outgoing mail can go by ordinary or registered post, courier, e-mail or dispatch rider.

questions.stem:
(a) Define filing. [2 marks]
(b) State four purposes of filing. [8 marks]
(c) Describe each of the following classifications of filing, stating one advantage of each: (i) alphabetical; (ii) numerical; (iii) subject. [6 marks]
(d) Name four items of filing equipment. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) the systematic arrangement and storage of documents so that they can be found easily when needed
8 marks: (b) any four, 2 marks each: safe keeping of documents; easy retrieval; keeping records for reference; legal evidence; confidentiality; orderly office
2 marks: (c)(i) alphabetical: files arranged in A-Z order of names; advantage: simple, no index needed
2 marks: (c)(ii) numerical: each file given a number and arranged in number order; advantage: easy expansion, more confidential
2 marks: (c)(iii) subject: files arranged by topic; advantage: all papers on one subject are together
4 marks: (d) any four: filing cabinet, box file, lever arch file, folders, shelves/racks, card index, computer (1 mark each)
questions.explanation: Filing is the systematic storage of documents. It keeps them safe, accessible, confidential and available as evidence. Alphabetical filing is simple; numerical is expandable and confidential but needs an index; subject filing groups related papers. Equipment includes cabinets, box files and lever arch files.

questions.stem:
(a) Define communication. [2 marks]
(b) State four importance of communication in an office. [8 marks]
(c) Distinguish between verbal and non-verbal communication, giving two examples of each. [6 marks]
(d) Name two communication service providers in Nigeria. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) the transfer of information, ideas or messages from a sender to a receiver with understanding
8 marks: (b) any four, 2 marks each: passing instructions; coordinating departments; decision making; good relations with customers; motivating staff; feedback
2 marks: (c) verbal communication uses words, spoken or written
1 mark: (c) examples of verbal: e.g. telephone conversation, letter, meeting, memo
2 marks: (c) non-verbal communication uses signs, gestures, pictures or sounds without words
1 mark: (c) examples of non-verbal: e.g. gestures, facial expression, charts, sirens
4 marks: (d) any two: NIPOST, GSM network operators, Internet service providers, broadcasting stations/media houses, satellite service providers (2 marks each)
questions.explanation: Communication passes messages from sender to receiver. In an office it carries instructions, coordinates work, aids decisions and builds relations. Verbal communication uses words (telephone, letter); non-verbal uses gestures and visuals. Providers include NIPOST, GSM operators and ISPs.

questions.stem:
The Principal of Unity Secondary School, Ilorin, has asked you, as school secretary, to arrange a staff meeting.
(a) State four duties of the secretary before the meeting. [8 marks]
(b) Arrange the following items in their correct order of business: matters arising; any other business; reading of the last minutes; chairman's opening remarks; main business; adjournment. [6 marks]
(c) Explain the following terms: (i) quorum; (ii) motion; (iii) proxy. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
8 marks: (a) any four, 2 marks each: prepare the agenda with the chairman; send notice of meeting; book the venue; prepare documents/previous minutes; arrange seating and materials; inform members of the date and time
6 marks: (b) chairman's opening remarks; reading of the last minutes; matters arising; main business; any other business; adjournment (1 mark for each correct position)
2 marks: (c)(i) quorum: the minimum number of members that must be present for the meeting to be valid
2 marks: (c)(ii) motion: a formal proposal put before a meeting for discussion and decision
2 marks: (c)(iii) proxy: a person authorised to attend and vote on behalf of a member, or the document giving that authority
questions.explanation: Before the meeting the secretary prepares the agenda, sends notices, books the venue and prepares papers. Order: chairman's remarks, last minutes, matters arising, main business, AOB, adjournment. Quorum is the minimum attendance; a motion is a formal proposal; a proxy votes for an absent member.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain the meaning of a report. [2 marks]
(b) Describe four types of formal report. [8 marks]
(c) List six parts of a formal report. [6 marks]
(d) State two importance of report writing. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) a formal written account of facts, findings or events, often with conclusions and recommendations, presented to a person or body that requested it
2 marks: (b) short report: brief, on a simple issue
2 marks: (b) long report: detailed, on a complex issue, with sections
2 marks: (b) investigative report: written after looking into a specific problem or incident
2 marks: (b) routine/periodic report: written at regular intervals, e.g. monthly
6 marks: (c) any six: title; terms of reference; introduction; procedure/method; findings; conclusion; recommendations; signature and date; appendix (1 mark each)
4 marks: (d) any two, 2 marks each: helps decision making; provides records; informs management; evaluates performance
questions.explanation: A report is a formal written account of findings. Types: short, long, investigative and routine. Parts: title, terms of reference, introduction, method, findings, conclusion, recommendations, signature and date. Reports aid decisions and keep records.

questions.stem:
Mrs Okonkwo, the sales manager of a soft-drink company in Aba, complains that the sales figures she receives each month are late and often contain errors.
(a) Define information. [2 marks]
(b) Identify the two qualities of good information that are lacking in the case above and explain each. [6 marks]
(c) State four other qualities of good information. [4 marks]
(d) State four sources of information available to an organisation. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) processed data that is meaningful and useful to the receiver for decision making
3 marks: (b) timeliness: information should reach the user in time for the decision
3 marks: (b) accuracy: information should be correct and free from errors
4 marks: (c) any four: relevance; completeness; clarity/usability; conciseness; reliability; cost-effectiveness (1 mark each)
8 marks: (d) any four, 2 marks each: internal records; staff reports; questionnaires and interviews; newspapers and magazines; Internet; government publications; reference books
questions.explanation: Information is processed, meaningful data. The case shows lack of timeliness and accuracy. Other qualities: relevance, completeness, clarity and conciseness. Sources: internal records, reports, surveys, newspapers, the Internet, government publications.
